rows.verified: Employers must assess vibration risks to employees to identify whether a problem exists.
Appropriate control measures must be introduced to reduce vibration risks.
Health surveillance is required for hand-arm vibration where risk remains.
Employees must receive information and training about vibration risks and the controls being used.
Hand-arm vibration can arise from hand-held tools, hand-guided equipment and hand-fed machines.
Whole-body vibration is transmitted through the seat or feet of workers driving mobile machinery or work vehicles over rough surfaces.
Hand-arm vibration syndrome can affect nerves, blood vessels, muscles and joints and can reduce grip strength and sense of touch.
Risk reduction can include alternative work methods, lower-vibration equipment, suitable maintenance and limiting exposure time.
Vibration controls depend on the tool or vehicle, vibration magnitude, exposure duration, maintenance, posture and worker health.
Vibration evidence is equipment-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
Manual handling includes lifting, putting down, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving a load by hand or bodily force.
Hazardous manual handling should be avoided so far as reasonably practicable.
Hazardous manual handling operations that cannot be avoided must be assessed.
The risk of injury from unavoidable hazardous manual handling must be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.
The law does not set a single specific weight limit for manual handling.
Where reasonably practicable and relevant to injury risk, information should be provided about load weight and centre of gravity.
Hazardous handling can be avoided by redesigning the task so the load does not need to be moved.
Automation, conveyors, pallet trucks, hoists and lift trucks can reduce or eliminate manual-handling risk.
Manual-handling risk depends on the task, individual, load, environment, frequency, posture and available mechanical aids.
Manual-handling evidence is task-, load- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level musculoskeletal-injury probability.
